Newborn Care

Could a baby have haemorrhoids?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Haemorrhoids can occur in young children, but they are uncommon in babies. A small tear, irritated skin or another condition is often a more likely explanation for blood or a bump around the anus. Do not diagnose the cause from a photograph or start an adult haemorrhoid treatment without advice.

What else could explain the symptoms?

Haemorrhoids are enlarged vascular cushions in the anal canal or around the anal opening; internal and external haemorrhoids describe their location. Although pressure and straining can contribute, the common adult risk list (including pregnancy or prolonged toilet sitting) does not explain a baby’s symptoms by itself.

An anal fissure is a small tear near the opening of the anus. A hard stool can cause it, and you may notice a little bright-red blood on the stool or when wiping. Passing another hard stool can hurt and reopen the area.

A skin tag can also look like a small bump. Bleeding mixed with loose stools, mucus, a tender swelling or persistent symptoms may have another cause. The appearance alone cannot distinguish a fissure, infection, food-protein-related inflammation or other bowel condition.

Contact your baby’s healthcare professional about any suspected rectal bleeding or new lump. Explain your baby’s age, feeding, stool consistency and whether they seem otherwise well. A photograph of the nappy or a saved sample, if the team requests one, can help describe what happened.

When the assessment is urgent

Seek prompt medical care for any blood in the stool of a baby under three months, or for bleeding with diarrhoea, significant pain, persistent crying, a very unwell appearance or unexplained bruising. A small streak in an otherwise well older baby still warrants medical advice.

Black, tar-like stool outside the normal newborn meconium period needs urgent assessment. Heavy bleeding, collapse, difficulty waking, repeated green vomit or a swollen painful abdomen requires emergency care. A fever of 38°C or more in a baby younger than three months also needs urgent assessment.

Do not wait one or two weeks to see whether home treatment works before reporting blood. A minor fissure is a common possibility, but its presence should be established rather than assumed.

Straining does not always mean constipation

Young babies may grunt, turn red or cry before passing a soft stool while they learn to coordinate pushing and relaxing. This can be infant dyschezia rather than constipation. It does not by itself mean a vein is being damaged or that a suppository is needed.

Hard, dry stools and difficulty passing them are more suggestive of constipation. Stool frequency alone is not enough: some breastfed babies pass soft stools infrequently after the early weeks. In a very young baby, infrequent stools can also prompt a feeding and growth review.

Do not routinely stimulate the anus with a thermometer, cotton bud or other object to make a baby poo. Suppositories and rectal stimulation are not recommended for ordinary infant dyschezia. If you are unsure which pattern you are seeing, ask your clinician to assess it.

Make feeding changes appropriate to age

Continue normal milk feeds while seeking advice. Prepare formula using the exact water-to-powder ratio on the pack; adding extra powder or diluting it can be harmful. Ready-to-feed formula should not be watered down.

Babies under six months generally do not need extra water or juice beyond breast milk or correctly prepared formula unless a clinician specifically recommends it. If constipation treatment includes a small amount of fluid, ask for the exact type, amount and duration for your baby.

For a baby already eating complementary foods, age-appropriate fruit, vegetables and other fibre-containing foods may help keep stools softer. Introduce suitable textures and maintain milk feeding. Do not start solids early, make major dietary exclusions or repeatedly switch formula to treat unexplained bleeding.

For an infant who is already ready for solids, options might include appropriately textured peas, prunes or other fruit and oat or barley cereal. A clinician may occasionally suggest a measured amount of apple, pear or prune juice for constipation, but this is treatment advice for a particular age and situation, not a routine newborn drink.

Treatment follows the diagnosis

A clinician may recommend a stool-softening plan if constipation is causing a fissure or other discomfort. The medicine and dose depend on age and the assessment. Do not give an enema, laxative, glycerin suppository or haemorrhoid cream unless the clinician has advised it for this child.

Handle the area gently during nappy changes and ask which skin product, if any, is suitable. Do not insert petroleum jelly or medication into the anus as a routine way to help stools pass. A painful or enlarging swelling needs review rather than squeezing or trying to push it back.

Ask when improvement is expected and what to do if bleeding returns. Keeping stools comfortably soft can prevent another fissure, but ongoing symptoms may require a different diagnosis or specialist review.

Change dirty nappies promptly and clean with water or a suitable soft, fragrance-free wipe without scrubbing. Gentle leg movements may be soothing when your baby is comfortable, but they are not a treatment for rectal bleeding or a painful lump.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Paediatric guidance stresses that haemorrhoids are uncommon in babies and that blood or a new anal lump requires assessment for more likely causes.

AAP and paediatric services distinguish straining before a soft stool from constipation and recommend age-specific feeding and medicine advice rather than routine rectal stimulation.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare feeding, stool and symptom information for your baby’s clinician. A photograph cannot establish the cause of bleeding.

When to seek help

Report suspected blood in the stool. A very young or unwell baby, severe pain, green vomiting, a swollen abdomen, marked sleepiness or heavy bleeding needs urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Haemorrhoids are uncommon in babies; fissures and other causes need consideration.
  • Report blood in the nappy, with urgent care for a young or unwell baby.
  • Straining before a soft stool is not automatically constipation.
  • Use age-specific feeding and treatment advice rather than adult remedies.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use an adult haemorrhoid cream?

Not without a clinician’s advice. The diagnosis, ingredients and suitability for a baby must be checked.

Does crying while pooing mean haemorrhoids?

No. Stool consistency, feeding, examination and other symptoms help identify the cause.

Should I give water to a newborn with hard stools?

Ask a clinician first. Do not dilute formula or replace normal milk feeds with water.

Can a tiny blood streak be ignored?

It may come from a small fissure, but it still needs medical advice, especially in a baby under three months.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
